description: This team has been created to improve the skills and make appliances of the knowledge related to programming, and to improve the systems that already exist.
summary:
Earth Trend Detective is an interactive Python tool that turns 25 years of NASA satellite data into clear answers about how our planet is changing. We applied it to vegetation greenness (NDVI) around San Juan, an arid region of Argentina, using NASA MODIS data from 2001 to 2025 at 250 m resolution.

The tool addresses the challenge by letting users explore a satellite variable over time and see what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. It calculates a trend for every point on the map with three complementary statistical methods and a correction for false positives. Only significant changes are shown in color, and everything else is greyed out. Users click any area to get its time series and a one-sentence plain-language conclusion, such as whether it is greening or browning.

This matters because satellite data are open but hard to use, and a trend on a chart is not always a real change. Our tool makes the evidence visible and understandable for planners, students and communities, using only free NASA data and open-source software.
details:
What it does and how it works

Earth Trend Detective is an interactive Python application that turns 25 years of NASA satellite observations into clear answers to four questions: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant or just natural variability. We applied it to vegetation greenness (NDVI) around San Juan, Argentina, an arid region where vegetation depends on irrigation and rainfall.

The data are NASA MODIS/Terra MOD13Q1 v6.1 composites (250 m resolution, one every 16 days, 2001–2025) with their pixel-reliability quality layer, obtained through NASA AppEEARS. The tool removes unreliable pixels (clouds, fill values), reduces each year to an annual mean or peak NDVI, and then calculates a trend for every cell of the map using three complementary methods: an ordinary least squares slope adjusted for autocorrelation, the robust Theil–Sen estimator with a 95% confidence interval, and the Mann–Kendall test. Because thousands of cells are tested at once, we apply a Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction, and every cell that is not significant is greyed out on the map.

Users click any area to see its time series, trend lines, statistics and a one-sentence plain-language conclusion (for example, whether the area is greening or browning and by how much per decade). Sliders change the analysis window and region size, and a button exports the figure and the data as PNG and CSV.

Benefits and intended impact

The tool makes satellite time series accessible to people without remote-sensing training, such as local planners, water and agriculture managers, students and teachers, while giving researchers a transparent, reproducible workflow. In our run for 2009–2025, 18% of the cells showed a statistically significant change, with browning concentrated in parts of the area around the city. Such maps can help prioritize field checks and discussion about land use and water. Because it relies only on free NASA data and open-source software, any community can reuse it by changing the study area.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Python with NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio and Matplotlib, developed in PyCharm. Data access through NASA AppEEARS and Earthdata. The first prototype used NASA GISS temperature data (GISTEMP) before we adapted it to vegetation. It was developed and run on a desktop PC with an AMD Ryzen 5 5600GT and 24 GB of RAM, with no dedicated GPU. To keep it light, the tool processes one year at a time and can crop large downloads to the study area.

What makes it creative

Instead of showing only a map of trends, the tool shows how much we can trust each result. Non-significant cells are greyed out, three independent methods are compared, short analysis windows trigger a warning, and every result is summarized in plain language. We also validated the statistics on synthetic data with planted greening and browning patches, and checked that the tool found them and produced almost no false detections.

Factors we considered

We considered multiple-testing errors, autocorrelation between years, record length, cloud and quality filtering, and excluding the incomplete year 2026. We were also careful about interpretation: NDVI shows that greenness changed, not why. The patterns are consistent with urban expansion or land-use change, but confirming a cause needs other data, which we list as future work together with rainfall, temperature and seasonal analysis.
